summary: Specifies an RSVP-TE signaling extension to support ATM service class-aware MPLS traffic engineering, letting path setup account for the ATM service class. It is informational.

eli5.summary: ATM networks have different classes of service, like first class and coach. This adds a field so MPLS path setup can ask for the right class.

questions: atm service class mpls traffic engineering
how to signal atm class in mpls
subtitle: An RSVP-TE extension for signaling ATM service class requirements in label-switched paths.

tldr.problem: ATM networks support different service classes (CBR, VBR, UBR) with different QoS guarantees, but MPLS traffic engineering lacks a standard way to signal which class a path must support.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3496 defines the ATM_SERVICECLASS object for RSVP-TE PATH messages, letting senders specify the required ATM service class (UBR, VBR-NRT, VBR-RT, or CBR) when setting up label-switched paths.
tldr.outcome: This allows MPLS networks to carry ATM cells or emulate ATM service classes while leveraging MPLS traffic engineering capabilities, enabling ATM-aware label path setup.

today: RFC 3496 is an Informational document that specified an RSVP-TE extension for ATM service class signaling in MPLS networks. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference for implementations requiring ATM service class awareness in label-switched path setup.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 3496 defines a signaling extension for RSVP-TE (Resource ReSerVation Protocol - Traffic Engineering) to support ATM service classes in MPLS networks. The extension allows label-switched routers (LSRs) to signal which ATM service class a path must support when establishing label-switched path (LSP) tunnels.

The mechanism is agnostic to link types: it works with Ethernet, SONET, ATM links, and others. The RFC does not specify how to implement ATM service class behavior (such as queuing and scheduling); it only defines how to request that a path support a particular class. A key use case is carrying ATM cells encapsulated in MPLS packets to use MPLS networks as replacements for ATM networks.
sections.eli5: Routers need to tell each other what kind of service quality they need for a path, just like a shipping company picks express or standard delivery. This document shows how to include that request in MPLS setup messages.

sections.title: The ATM_SERVICECLASS Object
sections.content:
The ATM_SERVICECLASS object is a new RSVP-TE object included in PATH messages used to establish LSP tunnels. It is optional, so RSVP-TE implementations that do not need ATM service class support do not have to recognize it.

The object has a Class Number of 227 and contains a 3-bit Service Class (SC) field that specifies the desired ATM class: 0 for UBR (Unspecified Bit Rate), 1 for VBR-NRT (Variable Bit Rate, Non-Real Time), 2 for VBR-RT (Variable Bit Rate, Real Time), and 3 for CBR (Constant Bit Rate). The remaining 29 bits are reserved and must be set to zero. If multiple ATM_SERVICECLASS objects appear in a message, only the first is meaningful; subsequent ones are ignored.
sections.eli5: The object is a small tag in the setup message that says which class the path needs. It has four possible values for different service quality levels, plus some spare bits for future use.

sections.title: Handling and Non-support
sections.content:
When a sender LSR wants to establish an LSP with ATM service class support, it includes the ATM_SERVICECLASS object in the PATH message with the SC field set to the desired class. Each LSR along the path that recognizes this object records it in the path state block.

The destination LSR responds with a RESV message but does not include an ATM_SERVICECLASS object, regardless of whether the PATH message contained one. LSRs that do not recognize the ATM_SERVICECLASS class number or C-Type follow standard RSVP error procedures: they may ignore the object and forward it unchanged (if the class number format allows), or they may send a PathErr message with an 'Unknown object C-Type' error toward the sender, causing the path setup to fail.
sections.eli5: The sender puts the class request in the setup message. Routers that understand it remember it. If a router does not understand it, the setup may fail, and the sender should try again without the request or check what went wrong.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: RFC 3496 states that the ATM_SERVICECLASS extension does not add specific security requirements beyond those of Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) and existing MPLS traffic engineering. The security mechanisms already used with Diff-Serv and MPLS TE are sufficient to protect this extension.
sections.eli5: This addition does not introduce new security risks because the security methods already used for MPLS path setup work fine here too.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: The IANA has assigned RSVP Class Number 227 to the ATM_SERVICECLASS object. This class number identifies the object type in RSVP-TE messages and ensures there is no conflict with other RSVP object types.
sections.eli5: The Internet authority registered an official identification number for this new object type so that all implementations can recognize it the same way.
